note: Real material, arrived at by accident: an animal-sounds article crossed the operator's desk mid-session and three of its word-origin claims looked wrong. Running them past jeles' corroboration bar and into this store found something neither package's own tests had. Written with no `pr` key, per IDEAS 6.43 — the builder turns that field into every row's origin, so a guessed number puts a pull request that does not exist into the store's provenance. Assigned 57 when the PR opened.

decisions.question: Why use a stray magazine article as test material rather than a designed fixture?
decisions.commitment: Because the answers were not known when it started, and three of the four claims turned out to be wrong.
decisions.why: A designed fixture encodes what its author already believes. This one produced a spread nobody chose: two plain errors, one claim contradicted by its own earliest attestation, and one the article got right. The row that got it right is kept deliberately — a demo where the checker is correct about everything has its thumb on the scale, and a test pins that exactly one claim is recorded as holding.

decisions.question: What did running the claims past jeles' independence rule find?
decisions.commitment: Two of the ribbit row's six domains are the article being checked and a post quoting it nearly verbatim. The rule counts them as two independent sources.
decisions.why: MIN_INDEPENDENT_SOURCES counts distinct registrable domains, so wordsmarts.com and x.com clear the bar while carrying one claim twice. Measured by running it, not by reading the rule.

decisions.question: Is that a defect in jeles?
decisions.commitment: No, and the entry must not pretend it is. _independence.py already calls its own bar 'a cheap heuristic, deliberately weaker' so that nothing built on it borrows authority it has not earned.
decisions.why: The disclaimer describes one actor holding two domains. What was measured is a different and far more common shape needing no bad faith at all: one text republished. New is the concrete instance, not the weakness.

decisions.question: Could a blocklist close it, the way _NON_WITNESS closed the search-engine case?
decisions.commitment: No. The domain to exclude is different for every claim and is only knowable once you know where the claim came from.
decisions.why: _NON_WITNESS works because the search engine is the same for every query — jeles verified that an unfiltered count read DuckDuckGo as a source about every claim. Self-citation is provenance rather than a list, and a corroboration count has no access to the provenance of the claim it is scoring. Three options are recorded in IDEAS 6.47 and none is picked: pass the source domain in so it can exclude itself; compare citation text and count near-duplicates once, which is a matcher problem this repo already has one for; or accept it and let the seal carry the weight.

decisions.question: Three of the four findings are correct and well-sourced. Were any sealed?
decisions.commitment: None. Zero sealed, and a test pins that the demo contains no status='sealed' and no verifier= at all.
decisions.why: This is exactly the situation where a demo rewards itself: the machine was right, the evidence agreed, and nobody had checked. Being right is not being checked. A demo that sealed its own well-sourced readings would be the machine grading its own work in the file that exists to explain why that is forbidden.

decisions.question: Why are the citations pasted in rather than fetched at run time?
decisions.commitment: So it runs offline and deterministically, and so it does not route around somebody else's gate.
decisions.why: jeles keeps network access behind jeles._egress deliberately. A demo that quietly opened sockets to reproduce a number would be working around that, and a demo whose output changed with search rankings would not be a fixture. The URLs are the ones a real search actually returned.

decisions.question: How was the demo shown to be a gate rather than a description?
decisions.why: Sealing its own findings; dropping the article's own URL from the ribbit citations, which would leave a tidy six-source corroboration and no finding; disabling the self-citation detection; and making the checker right about every claim. The second is the one worth naming — the trap is data in the fixture, and quietly removing that URL would erase the result while leaving every other assertion green.
